title: Types vs Interfaces: why Matt Pocock reversed his 2022 take and now defaults to interface extends
summary: Matt revisits his 2022 types-vs-interfaces video and corrects it. The real performance issue is interface extends versus intersections, not type versus interface for a plain object. He now defaults to interface for extending, and says single-object choice barely matters.

principles.text: The TypeScript perf advice contrasts interface extends with intersections, not types with interfaces; declaring a basic object either way has no performance difference.
principles.quote: Declaring an interface and a type just as a basic object are not going to give you any performance differences. It's about when you smoosh object types together.

principles.text: Interface extends is faster than intersections because TypeScript checks each hierarchical level and errors on incompatible properties rather than silently producing never.
principles.quote: This hierarchical relationship means that TypeScript is able to check at each level. Whereas when you smoosh these guys together with the intersection, it's not quite so easy for TypeScript.

principles.text: Intersections used repeatedly across a large codebase, such as extending a button's props, can wreck type-checking performance; interface extends gave Sentry a big speedup.
principles.quote: They halved their compile times and made the developer experience instantly reflect type changes.

principles.text: Default to interface extends over intersections when composing object types.
principles.quote: I think that just the thing you need to remember is default to interface extends over intersections.

principles.text: Interface declaration merging is a risk, but a lint rule (no-unsafe-declaration-merging) handles it, so it is not a big deal.
principles.quote: You can handle the edge cases with declaration merging with an ESLint rule.

principles.text: Interfaces are not assignable to index-signature record types because they could later be extended, whereas type aliases are; this edge case comes up rarely.
principles.quote: The reason for this is that an interface could later be extended. In other words, it could be declaration merged by something else.
